/intervals/11.note: ALICE's own detector is being upgraded in this shutdown: the ITS3 (replacing the three innermost tracking layers) and the FoCal forward calorimeter. CERN news of 25 April 2024, written by the ALICE collaboration, says the two upgrades 'have recently been approved for installation during the next long shutdown of the LHC'. The ALICE Collaboration's January 2026 paper (arXiv:2601.07405) says 'During the LHC Long Shutdown 3 (2026-29) ALICE will replace its three innermost tracking layers by a new detector'. ALICE's site says 'Further detector upgrades are being carried out for Run 4 until the end of 2033'; that describes the upgrade programme for Run 4 and does not date the end of this shutdown. The 2024 and 2026 ALICE-related sources give LS3 as 2026-28 and 2026-29; this interval follows CERN's later schedule, in which the LHC resumes operation in mid-2030. Work is under way: CERN's Long Shutdown 3 page reports 'Work on the CMS muon system upgrade is now underway' (17 September 2026) and 'The core of the CMS experiment, the pixel detector, has now been removed after 10 years of successful operations.' (19 October 2026). Start and end are the LHC-wide Long Shutdown 3 dates. CERN's 5 August 2026 item says 'The cryogenics team has been running the warm-up sequence since LS3 began on 29 June 2026' and that the stored helium is kept 'ready to be used again once the accelerator resumes operation in mid-2030'; CERN's 29 June 2026 article says 'The HiLumi LHC, scheduled to begin operation in 2030'. The end is a schedule value, not a reported event.
/intervals/10.quote: In the LHC caverns, the ATLAS and CMS experiments will undergo extensive upgrades, effectively becoming renewed detectors.

/intervals/10/end.note: CERN schedule: the LHC resumes operation in mid-2030; the rest of the CERN complex restarts in stages from mid-2028.

The value 1478 m is a unit conversion, not a depth measured for DUNE: 4850 ft x 0.3048 m/ft = 1478.3 m. For the metric figure, SURF's page on the MAJORANA Demonstrator (a different experiment, cited here only for the depth of the level in metres; DUNE is not mentioned on it) says "will be located at the 4850 Level (1478 m) Davis Campus at the Sanford Lab Underground Research Facility (SURF)." DUNE's own documents round the depth: the TDR glossary defines 4850L as "The depth in feet (1480 m) of the top of the cryostats underground at SURF" and Vol. I §1.3.1 says "approximately 1.5 km underground". SURF's scientific director rounds it to 1500 m in the Snowmass 2022 paper ("campuses at the 4850-foot level (1500 m, 4300 m.w.e.)") and gives 1490 m in a 2024 paper. The water-equivalent overburden is the separate 4300 m.w.e. value.

/intervals/1.note: Start = date_approved (1998-09-17). End = INSPIRE's date_completed field, which reads '2008-09'. That field is not a routine construction-milestone field: on ATLAS's INSPIRE record (1108541) and on LHCf's (1126263) the same field reads '9999', which both records treat as INSPIRE's placeholder for 'ongoing, not completed' rather than a real date. LHCb is likewise an active, non-terminal experiment, so a literal 'completed' date is implausible; the value is most likely either an INSPIRE data-entry anomaly or a differently scoped milestone (for example detector installation or construction complete, consistent with first collisions 14 months later). No source independent of this one INSPIRE field corroborates a September 2008 construction-complete date for LHCb, so confidence is 'uncertain' and the interval is given the non-terminal status 'construction', not 'completed'; it must not be read as asserting that LHCb completed in 2008. The LHCb JINST detector paper or an LHCb-specific installation announcement would settle it.

/intervals/8.locator: home.cern/science/long-shutdown-3, item of 5 August 2026 "The LHC is being warmed up from near absolute zero to room temperature"
/intervals/8.note: LHCb's own detector is being enhanced in this shutdown: the inner part of the electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL) is replaced and the RICH electronics are upgraded. LHCb's outreach site (8 May 2024) says 'The LHCb experiment will upgrade the inner part of the Electromagnetic Calorimeter and the electronics of the Ring Imaging Cherenkov detectors in the next LHC Long Shutdown (LS3)'. The LHCb ECAL group's JINST paper (published 11 March 2026) says 'An enhancement of the LHCb electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL) is foreseen during Long Shutdown 3 (LS3) of the LHC' and 'In total, 176 new SpaCal modules with radiation-tolerant scintillating plastic fibers will be installed during LS3'. These are plans for the shutdown; no source consulted reports the installation as under way or finished. The main Upgrade II is a later step: 'Upgrade II will be installed during Long Shutdown 4 (LS4)' (LHCb outreach site, 2024). The 2024 page gives LS3 as 'currently scheduled for the years 2026–28'; this interval follows CERN's later schedule, in which the LHC resumes operation in mid-2030. Start and end are the LHC-wide Long Shutdown 3 dates. CERN's 5 August 2026 item says 'The cryogenics team has been running the warm-up sequence since LS3 began on 29 June 2026' and that the stored helium is kept 'ready to be used again once the accelerator resumes operation in mid-2030'; CERN's 29 June 2026 article says 'The HiLumi LHC, scheduled to begin operation in 2030'. The end is a schedule value, not a reported event.
/intervals/8.quote: The LHCb experiment will upgrade the inner part of the Electromagnetic Calorimeter and the electronics of the Ring Imaging Cherenkov detectors in the next LHC Long Shutdown (LS3).

/intervals/8/end.note: CERN schedule: the LHC resumes operation in mid-2030; the rest of the CERN complex restarts in stages from mid-2028.

/intervals/4.note: Derived from the beam source: NuMI, the only beam NOvA uses, has not run since July 2024 (see beamline:numi). Restart is a plan, not a report: the PAC report of the April 2026 meeting (posted June 2026) says "A 20 week run is planned from October 2026 to Feb 2027 to run NuMI. The long shutdown is planned for 2028-29." It adds that the repaired transformers were due by 15 September, two weeks before the 1 October NuMI start. No source dated after July 2026 was found that confirms the restart, so the shutdown is left in place at 2026-10-25 and should be re-checked. The rest of the complex (Linac, Booster, Booster Neutrino Beam) kept running. UPDATE 2026-10-25: the PAC report of the 1-4 September 2026 meeting (posted October 2026) still lists the restart as a plan: "Beam has already been established in Linac and Booster (Aug 26), MI will start up on September 21, stable beam is planned for October 1"; 6 of 8 transformers operational. No source dated after 21 September was reachable, so the shutdown is kept. CONFLICTING STATEMENT (left unresolved, status kept): Fermilab's 7 July 2026 feature says NOvA 'is the only currently operating long-baseline neutrino experiment in the United States' and 'is taking data' (https://news.fnal.gov/2026/07/fermilab-marks-70-years-of-neutrino-science-and-leads-next-generation-experiment/); the PAC reports (April and September 2026) are more specific that the Main Injector has not delivered NuMI beam since July 2024, and the feature does not say which data. Shutdown here means no NuMI beam data-taking, not that the detectors are powered down.
/intervals/4.quote: Following the record achievement, the Main Injector complex suffered a series of failures that have prevented NuMI beam.

/intervals/5.note: A schedule, not a reported event. April 2026 PAC report: a 20-week run planned October 2026 to February 2027 (FY27 NuMI run already cut from 30 to 20 weeks for budget; the PAC thought 12 weeks would suffice). Sept 2026 PAC report: "The plan is for 12 weeks of operation in FY27, with a stretch goal of 20 weeks of operation, with a focus on the NuMI beam"; MI start-up planned 2026-09-21, stable beam 2026-10-01. Whether the run started is not confirmed by any fetched source as of 2026-10-25. The planned end (2027-02) is the 20-week stretch case from the April report; a 12-week run from 1 October would end near the end of December 2026.

/geometry.note: CONUS's own paper (arXiv:2401.07684) states the detector sat 17.1 m from the reactor core center at Brokdorf, inside the reactor building itself (not a separate structure). No source consulted gives the azimuth of that 17.1 m offset from the core, so this point is the centroid of the OSM 'Reaktorgebäude' building (geometry:brokdorf-core), used directly as the detector's position. The stated accuracy is 40 m: the unresolved 17.1 m offset plus up to about 21 m between the polygon centroid and the reactor axis (a circle fitted to the 13 vertices of the polygon's circular arc, radius 40.2 m, residual <= 2.7 m, is centred 20.4 m SSW of the centroid, at 9.3457897 E 53.8505931 N; no source states whether that arc is concentric with the core).

/geometry.locator: arXiv:1003.1391 Table 1.2 (per-reactor near/far baselines); OSM reactor-building positions
/geometry.note: Nonlinear least-squares multilateration (scipy.optimize.least_squares on raw Euclidean centre-to-centre distance residuals, local equirectangular projection) of this detector hall's position from the six Hanbit reactor-core buildings (geometry:hanbit-core-r1..r6; accuracy_m 8 each), using the per-reactor near/far distances published in the RENO proposal (arXiv:1003.1391, Table 1.2, 'Distances of the reactor cores from the near and far detectors'). Of all 6! possible assignments of the table's R1-R6 labels to the six OSM buildings (and the reflection of the whole line), only the natural southwest-to-northeast geographic numbering converges to a good fit (residual root-mean-square 3-5 m on baselines of 300-1560 m, i.e. well under 2%); every other assignment leaves a residual of hundreds of metres, so this numbering (not independently sourced -- the proposal gives no reactor coordinates) is adopted on that self-consistency alone. accuracy_m is set above the fit residual to also cover the OSM buildings' own ~8 m footprint accuracy and this table being the experiment's 2010 design/proposal figure rather than an as-built survey (the collaboration's own later papers confirm the same overall geometry only as flux-weighted averages: 294 m / 1383 m from the array centre, arXiv:1204.0626).
